item.title: Separating active irradiation from passive outcome learning in radiotherapy: a finite-model computational benchmark
item.description: arXiv:2610.14222v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Apparent gains from informative irradiation may reflect treatment reoptimization or better use of outcomes from static treatment. We tested whether changing irradiation adds value beyond optimized static treatment, passive outcome learning, and data-dependent stopping. Three synthetic three-dimensional geometries supplied 51 parent fluences. Four known response scenarios generated Bernoulli risks from normalized organ-dose contrasts at uncalibrated slopes of 0, 4, 16, and 64; one unknown scenario applied to all 2,816 hypothetical uses. Loss included acquisition and deployment. We compared fixed passive and locally selected fixed active sampling, passive optimal stopping, and a restricted one-checkpoint, one-switch active policy with a shared terminal menu. Fixed active sampling improved on fixed passive sampling in three of nine nonzero-slope conditions, but never on passive stopping. One-switch adaptation added at most 4.00625e-5 expected model events avoided. With the policies held fixed, two of four increments above the numerical reporting threshold reversed sign under alternative integration; all four became negative at some allowed prior weighting. Adding three generated probes changed none of 72 paired policy values, and none was used on a positive-probability path. The tested probes did not demonstrate stable incremental value beyond optimized passive stopping. Treatment opportunities, stopping permissions, acquisition costs, and input sensitivity must be separated when attributing benefits to active irradiation. These are restricted finite-model results, not evidence about unrestricted active learning or clinical safety and effectiveness.
item.dc:creator: Yuntao Wang

item.title: Automated carotid artery atherosclerotic inflammation segmentation in PET using MSR-Net
item.description: arXiv:2610.15245v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Objective. To develop an automated method for segmentation and uptake quantification of carotid atherosclerotic inflammation on 64Cu-CANF-comb PET while accounting for partial-volume and tissue-fraction effects. Approach. Synthetic carotid PET images with known fractional-volume ground truth were generated by combining MR-derived high-resolution activity maps with GATE Monte Carlo simulation incorporating major PET physical processes and matched to the Biograph mMR acquisition and reconstruction. A two-stage network first localized the carotid vessel wall from T1-weighted MR and then estimated voxel-wise inflammation fraction from masked PET. Both stages used a multiscale residual (MSR) convolutional backbone. Performance was compared with U-Net, Transformer U-Net, DUCK-Net, and iterative Yang partial-volume correction. Main results. In a two-alternative forced-choice study, five nuclear-medicine physicians identified real images with 54% accuracy (54/100; Wilson 95% CI 0.44-0.63; exact binomial p = 0.48). On 184 simulated test slices from five held-out patients, the proposed method achieved a weighted DSC of 0.79, compared with 0.73 for U-Net, 0.69 for Transformer U-Net, and 0.75 for DUCK-Net, with corresponding HD values of 1.85, 2.29, 2.32, and 2.23 voxels. Patient-cluster bootstrap comparisons favored the proposed method for DSC and HD against all three baselines (Holm-corrected p <= 0.031). Overall ENRMSE was 0.24 versus 0.59, 0.68, and 0.59 for the three DL baselines and 0.57 for iterative Yang. In seven patients, corrected SUV showed a positive association with MR-derived lipid-rich/necrotic core with hemorrhage. Significance. The proposed framework improved carotid PET segmentation and uptake quantification under simulated conditions. The patient analysis is preliminary and requires external validation with biological reference standards before clinical deployment.

item.title: Personalized Physiological-Model-Based Neural Network for Glucose Forecasting in Type 1 Diabetes
item.description: arXiv:2610.15456v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate, physiologically consistent glucose forecasts could help people with type 1 diabetes respond to impending excursions. We applied our physiological-model-based neural network (PMB--NN) framework to glucose forecasting. A temporal convolutional network (TCN) used 180 min of history, constrained during training by a personalized four-parameter physiological model. The main PMB--NN combined forecast and neural--physiological agreement losses; a three-term variant additionally fitted physiological predictions to measured glucose. Data comprised 6--8 weeks of continuous glucose monitoring, pump, and meal records from 25 AZT1D participants. Person-specific models used chronological 70/10/20 train/validation/test splits and 30-, 60-, and 120-min horizons. Median mean absolute errors were 16.24, 25.00, and 30.20 mg/dL with basal insulin records and 15.38, 24.21, and 31.79 mg/dL before these records became available. In the latter setting, PMB--NN had the lowest median error at 30 and 60 min; it outperformed the physiological model alone in all six settings. In input-increase tests, glucose predictions changed in the expected direction for 85\% of correction boluses and 100\% of carbohydrate rescues, versus 57\% for active insulin and 56\% for active carbohydrates. Most standalone physiological fits showed locally distinguishable parameter effects, with glucose-related coefficients more stable under resampling than insulin- or carbohydrate-related coefficients. The three-term variant improved hyperglycaemia accuracy with basal records, but did not significantly change overall MAE and reduced directional plausibility in three tests. PMB--NN combines personalized forecasting with an explicit physiological model, allowing assessment of predictive accuracy, physiological response behavior, and participant-specific coefficients.
item.dc:creator: Yaowen Zhang, Shuhao Que, Ying Wang

item.title: BOLD PSF: Impact of k-space trajectories and timing on the depiction of T2* contrast
item.description: arXiv:2610.15524v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The timing of BOLD-fMRI is typically chosen such that TE matches T2*. This assumes contrast being exclusively elicited by signal differences at TE. While sensible for short or TE-symmetric readouts, such as EPIs, it oversimplifies contrast generation for longer or TE-asymmetric trajectories, such as spirals. We propose the concept of a BOLD PSF for a more comprehensive perspective on the imaging characteristics of a functional experiment. Our findings indicate that TE can be reduced for spiral-out without sacrificing BOLD-sensitivity when compared to EPI. Furthermore, we characterize the intrinsic trade-off between specificity and resolution of the BOLD response under varying TE.
item.dc:creator: Maria Engel, Lars Kasper, Klaas P Pruessmann

item.title: Photoacoustic imaging of human brain function through intact adult skulls
item.description: arXiv:2610.17504v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) has revolutionized noninvasive imaging of human brain function, but it indirectly senses deoxyhemoglobin through water-proton relaxation and relies on bulky, costly, noisy, enclosed, superconducting-magnet scanners. In contrast, photoacoustic computed tomography (PACT) directly probes hemoglobin absorption using a more compact, lower-cost, quieter, open, magnet-free system. However, functional PACT of the adult human brain has so far been demonstrated only after surgical skull removal, because the skull strongly attenuates optical and acoustic signals. Here, we demonstrate non-invasive transcranial functional PACT (T-fPACT) through the intact adult skull. A densely packed, high-channel-count (3,072-element) hemispherical ultrasonic array provides near-$2\pi$-steradian simultaneous acquisition, enabling high sensitivity and single-shot three-dimensional imaging at 20 Hz that eliminates motion blurring. Participant-specific stabilization further enables measurement of small task-evoked hemodynamic responses over the entire task duration. In healthy adults, T-fPACT localized responses to expected sensorimotor regions, distinguished task-specific motor representations, and yielded consistent localizations across repeated task runs and visits. Comparison with high-field (7 T) fMRI showed spatially corresponding functional regions, while dual-wavelength imaging revealed distinct hemoglobin-weighted responses. These findings overcome the long-standing skull barrier in human brain PACT and establish non-invasive, rapid volumetric photoacoustic imaging of brain function.

item.title: Direct correlation of intravoxel incoherent motion imaging based on implicit neural representations and histopathology in pediatric Wilms tumors: can it differentiate between subtypes?
item.description: arXiv:2610.18728v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Wilms tumor (WT) is a heterogeneous pediatric renal malignancy. Invasive procedures to establish histology prior to pre operative treatment are not recommended by the International Society of Pediatric (SIOP) Oncology Renal Tumor Study Group, yet different tissue components are associated with different responses to therapy (SIOP Umbrella protocol). Intravoxel incoherent motion (IVIM) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) may improve subtype differentiation before surgery as a noninvasive radiographic biomarker by capturing both diffusion and perfusion characteristics, as opposed to the conventionally used apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC). The objective of this study is to evaluate the discriminative performance of IVIM MRI in differentiating WT subtypes. IVIM provides quantitative parameters that disentangle the diffusion coefficient (D), incoherent blood flow (pseudodiffusion Dstar) and perfusion fraction (f). This retrospective study included thirthy children with WT. Standardized 1.5T MRI with 10 b value diffusion weighted imaging (DWI) was performed. IVIM parameters were estimated using a selfsupervised implicit neural representations network and were correlated with histopathology via a patient specific 3D printed cutting guide. Statistical analyses included mixed models, receiver operating curve analysis, and logistic regression. Thirty lesions were MRI histopathology correlated on slice level. Significant subtype differences were observed for Dstar stromal versus epithelial (p = 0.024), regressive tumors (p = 0.031) and mixed WT tumors (p = 0.043). ADC showed no significant subtype differences. Direct MRI histopathology correlation enabled differentiation between stromal subtype and epithelial, mixed and regressive subtype on macroscopic slice level using Dstar.

item.title: Experimental Demonstration of Soft-Tissue Muon Scattering Tomography
item.description: arXiv:2610.16647v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Muons have fascinated physicists since their discovery in cosmic rays almost a century ago. Their large mass and relatively long lifetime allow relativistic muons to traverse large amounts of matter, a property that has been exploited to probe otherwise inaccessible structures, from volcanoes and archaeological monuments to shielded nuclear materials. Here, we experimentally demonstrate for the first time that muon scattering tomography can be extended to biological soft tissue. We image an anthropomorphic thorax phantom using a 2 GeV/c muon beam at the CERN Proton Synchrotron and reconstruct its three-dimensional scattering density from the measured deflections of individual muons. Despite the weak scattering produced by tissue-equivalent materials, the reconstructed density agrees with the expectation from simulation at the percent level. Our results extend muon imaging into a previously unexplored regime and open the possibility of using muons as a complementary probe for medical imaging.
item.dc:creator: Dipanwita Banerjee, Benjamin Banto Oberhauser, Paolo Crivelli, Laura Molina Bueno

item.title: Numerical simulation of biological capsules based on interface-fitted polygonal meshes
item.description: arXiv:2610.18172v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this work we introduce a numerical framework for the simulation of biological capsules based on meshes that adapt iteration-wise to the shape of the membrane. The discretization leverages a Hybrid High Order method (HHO) to solve a Stokes problem with a source term distributed on the interface between the internal and the external phases. The HHO discretization supports meshes composed of general polygons, permitting to use fitted meshes that can be easily generated by cutting the elements intersected by the interface. Moreover, polygonal meshes allow arbitrarily accurate interface discretizations without introducing bulk degrees of freedom. The presentation of the simulation algorithm is completed with a proof-of-concept numerical test on a well-established benchmark: the deformation of an elastic capsule immersed in a shear flow.
item.dc:creator: Daniele A. Di Pietro, Simon Mendez, Aurelio E. Spadotto

item.title: Hyperelastic Modeling of Cardiac Tissue Deformation for Data Registration
item.description: arXiv:2610.18207v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This work proposes a biomechanical registration framework designed to combine functional optical-mapping data with structural high-resolution MRI of cardiac tissue. The two acquisitions are performed in different mechanical configurations: optical mapping is obtained after stretching the sample, whereas MRI is acquired in a fixed resting state. To estimate the deformation between these configurations, the tissue is modeled as a nearly incompressible transversely isotropic hyperelastic material, and the traction amplitude is identified from optical-map marker positions through an inverse problem. Two-and threedimensional simulations show physically admissible deformations and provide a first proof of concept for the proposed strategy.

item.title: Racket Kinematics and Ball Performance During the Forehand Reverse Flick: A Pilot Comparison With the Backhand Flick in Table Tennis
item.description: arXiv:2601.07363v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Background Following changes in table tennis ball materials, offensive returns have become more important for initiating sustained topspin offense. However, using the backhand flick (BF) to return forehand short balls often increases the difficulty of recovery and continuity, revealing a technical gap. This study preliminarily verified a novel forehand short return technique, the forehand reverse flick (FRF), and analyzed its similarities and differences with the BF. Methods Four elite athletes completed seven consecutive days of FRF specific training. Infrared motion capture and ultra-high-speed cameras were used to collect data on racket kinematics, movement duration, and ball performance. Results The success rate of the FRF increased steadily, reaching 86%. Racket trajectories of the two techniques were highly similar along the X (r = 1) and Y (r = 0.99) axes but differed along the Z (r = -0.04) axis. Racket and ball velocities were comparable between techniques, whereas the FRF showed lower resultant acceleration (approximately 265.57 m/s) and required about 0.03 s more for movement duration. Ball velocity was comparable between techniques, for the ball spin, the FRF generated lower spin (approximately 76.61 r/s) about 64% of the BF value (approximately 120.13 r/s). The highest participant mean spin rate reached 93 r/s, about 77% of the BF mean. Conclusion Overall, the FRF was found to have favorable learnability and training value, with potential for further optimization and competitive application.
item.dc:creator: Pengfei Jin, Jie Ren, Chen Yang, Qingtao Kong, Qingshan Zhang, Nan Gu, Bin Chen, Qin Zhang, Zhe Feng

item.title: Continuous 3-D Latent Diffusion for Medical Image Generation and Reconstruction
item.description: arXiv:2607.16491v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: High-resolution three-dimensional (3-D) medical latent diffusion remains limited by the cost of decoding full volumes, which existing latent autoencoders (AEs) handle through overlapping sub-volume decoding. We propose a continuous 3-D latent diffusion model framework for computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) generation and measurement-guided reconstruction, built on a coordinate-rendering autoencoder (CoRe-AE). Its decoder applies its convolutional stage once on the compact latent grid and renders voxel intensities from spatial coordinates through a lightweight implicit head, evaluated in memory-bounded chunks. This design avoids overlapping sub-volumes and remains differentiable with respect to the latent, so that the decoder can be used inside measurement-guided reconstruction. The framework was evaluated on CT volumes of 512\textsuperscript{3} voxels and MRI volumes of 256\textsuperscript{3} voxels. At 512\textsuperscript{3}, the decoder was 4--18 times faster than the MAISI and 3D MedDiffusion AEs and required the lowest peak graphics processing unit (GPU) memory, including when its gradient was computed. CoRe-AE also achieved the highest peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and structural similarity index (SSIM) among the evaluated AEs on both modalities. The resulting frozen 3-D latent prior generated full volumes without patch seams and, without retraining, reconstructed sparse-view CT and accelerated MRI through hard data consistency, within 2.4--4.9 dB PSNR of the pixel-domain decomposed diffusion sampler (DDS). A single volumetric latent prior thus supports both generation and reconstruction of high-resolution medical volumes on one GPU. Our code will be made available at https://github.com/Mellak/continuous-3d-latent-diffusion/.
item.dc:creator: Youness Mellak, Antoine De Paepe, Dimitris Visvikis, Alexandre Bousse

item.title: MosaicMRI: A Diverse Dataset and Benchmark for Raw Musculoskeletal MRI
item.description: arXiv:2604.11762v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Deep learning underpins a wide range of applications in MRI, including reconstruction, artifact removal, and segmentation. However, progress has been driven largely by public datasets focused on brain and knee imaging, shaping how models are trained and evaluated. As a result, careful studies of the reliability of these models across diverse anatomical settings remain limited. In this work, we introduce MosaicMRI, a large and diverse collection of fully sampled raw musculoskeletal (MSK) MR measurements designed for training and evaluating machine-learning--based methods. MosaicMRI is the largest open-source raw MSK MRI dataset to date, comprising 3,150 volumes and 89,830 slices, including a 3,096-volume 1.5~T core dataset and a 54-volume 0.55~T low-field set. The dataset offers substantial diversity in volume orientation (e.g., axial, sagittal), imaging contrasts (e.g., PD, T1, T2), anatomies (e.g., spine, knee, hip, ankle, and others), numbers of acquisition coils, and field strengths. Using accelerated reconstruction as a testbed, we study scaling, robustness, and data selection under realistic MSK distribution shifts. Across E2E-VarNet, U-Net, and ViT baselines, mixed-anatomy training improves over anatomy-specific training, showing that the benefit of anatomical diversity is not architecture-specific. Zero-shot experiments on the 0.55~T low-field set highlight that using more training data improves average reconstruction under field-strength shift. Controlled subset experiments further suggest that these gains come from transferable cross-anatomy structure, rather than anatomy or contrast matching alone.
item.dc:creator: Paula Arguello, Berk Tinaz, Mohammad Shahab Sepehri, Maryam Soltanolkotabi, Mahdi Soltanolkotabi

item.title: GS-DOT: Gaussian splatting-based image reconstruction for diffuse optical tomography
item.description: arXiv:2604.23675v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This work presents GS-DOT, a novel image reconstruction framework based on Gaussian Splatting (GS) for diffuse optical tomography (DOT). Inspired by GS for rendering applications, absorption coefficients are represented as a sparse sum of anisotropic Gaussian primitives optimized to fit measured time-resolved point-spread functions through analytic gradients and Adam optimization. This is the first adaptation of GS algorithms in the photon diffusion regime, where the ray transport function is replaced by the diffusion functions to enable accurate modeling of light transport in highly scattering media. Validation on synthetic tissue models demonstrate high accuracy in localization and quantification of reconstructed absorption maps for both clean and noisy signals. GS-DOT has demonstrated high robustness to noise and showed a huge reduction in memory demand.
item.dc:creator: Jingjing Jiang
